title: Heparin: Bleeding, HIT, and Monitoring
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Unfractionated heparin prevents further clot formation but can cause major bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Safe care requires the correct route/concentration, protocol-based coagulation monitoring when therapeutic dosing is used, platelet trending, and immediate escalation for bleeding or new thrombosis with a platelet fall.
recognize: Unexpected bruising, hematuria, melena, hematemesis, hypotension, severe headache, or neurologic change can signal bleeding.
HIT is suspected when platelets fall substantially after heparin exposure, especially with new thrombosis; thrombosis can occur even while the platelet count is low.
priorities: Verify dose, concentration, route, indication, weight basis when applicable, and ordered laboratory monitoring.
Assess for active bleeding before and during therapy.
Stop heparin and escalate promptly when HIT is suspected according to protocol.
assessMonitor: Trend CBC/platelets, hemoglobin/hematocrit, bleeding, aPTT or anti-Xa when ordered for the regimen, renal status, and new thrombotic symptoms.
interventions: Use infusion-pump safeguards and independent double checks when required.
Apply prolonged pressure after invasive procedures and minimize unnecessary needle sticks.
medicationSafety: Protamine sulfate is used for heparin reversal when clinically indicated.
Heparin can contribute to hyperkalemia in susceptible patients, particularly with prolonged use.
Do not use the same assumptions for therapeutic heparin infusions and low-dose prophylactic regimens.
teaching: Report unusual bleeding, black stools, severe headache, or new limb pain/swelling immediately and avoid unapproved NSAIDs or supplements that increase bleeding.
delegationScope: Heparin administration and infusion management vary by state/facility for LPN/LVN practice; abnormal bleeding, platelet, or coagulation findings require licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Continuing heparin because the patient is clotting while ignoring a major platelet fall that suggests HIT.
oneLinePearl: Heparin can cause bleeding or paradoxical clotting from HIT—watch both.

title: Warfarin: INR, Bleeding, and Consistent Vitamin K
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic window and many drug/food interactions. INR monitoring, consistent—not absent—vitamin K intake, bleeding surveillance, and medication reconciliation are central to safe use.
recognize: Bleeding risk rises with supratherapeutic INR, interacting medications, acute illness, liver dysfunction, alcohol misuse, falls, and older age.
A sudden dietary change can alter anticoagulant effect; the goal is consistency rather than eliminating vitamin-K foods.
priorities: Verify the current INR and ordered dose plan when required before administration.
Assess for active bleeding, falls/head injury, new medications, antibiotics, and major dietary changes.
Escalate serious bleeding or markedly abnormal INR according to protocol.
assessMonitor: Trend INR, CBC, bleeding, bruising, stool/urine color, adherence, alcohol use, and medication/supplement changes.
interventions: Use bleeding precautions appropriate to risk and provide fall-prevention strategies.
Coordinate peri-procedural interruption or bridging only under the prescriber/anticoagulation plan.
medicationSafety: Vitamin K is used for reversal in selected situations; prothrombin complex concentrate may be used for life-threatening bleeding under emergency protocols.
Many antibiotics, antifungals, amiodarone, NSAIDs, antiplatelets, herbals, and alcohol can alter bleeding risk or INR.
teaching: Take the dose exactly as directed, keep INR appointments, maintain a consistent vitamin-K intake, and check before starting OTC drugs or supplements.
delegationScope: Medication administration may be within PN scope; dose adjustment and interpretation of INR-driven plans require authorized clinician review.
examTrap: Telling a patient on warfarin to stop eating all leafy green vegetables.
oneLinePearl: Warfarin safety is consistency plus INR surveillance.

title: Apixaban and Other DOACs: Bleeding Without Routine INR
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban reduce thromboembolic risk without routine INR titration, but bleeding risk remains significant. Adherence, renal/hepatic status, drug interactions, and procedure planning are key because missed doses rapidly reduce anticoagulant protection.
recognize: Bruising, epistaxis, hematuria, GI bleeding, anemia, or occult blood loss may occur.
Routine INR does not measure apixaban effect in the way it does warfarin.
priorities: Assess bleeding and verify indication, dose, renal/hepatic status, and interacting medications.
Escalate head injury or major bleeding urgently.
Confirm peri-procedural hold/restart timing from the treatment plan rather than guessing.
assessMonitor: Trend CBC, renal function, hepatic function when relevant, adherence, bleeding, falls, and medication changes.
interventions: Use fall-prevention and bleeding precautions appropriate to risk.
medicationSafety: Strong inhibitors or inducers of both CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein can alter apixaban exposure.
Abrupt discontinuation without alternative anticoagulation can increase thrombotic risk.
Reversal strategy depends on the specific DOAC and clinical situation.
teaching: Take doses on schedule and tell all clinicians/dentists about anticoagulant use; do not stop the medication independently.
delegationScope: Assessment of bleeding and appropriateness of dose/hold plans requires licensed clinician review.
examTrap: Using INR to decide whether apixaban is therapeutic.
oneLinePearl: DOACs skip routine INR—not bleeding surveillance.

title: Enoxaparin: Subcutaneous Anticoagulation Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Enoxaparin is a low-molecular-weight heparin used for VTE prevention and treatment. Safe care requires correct weight/renal dosing, proper abdominal subcutaneous technique, bleeding surveillance, and awareness that HIT can still occur.
recognize: Bleeding may present as bruising, hematuria, melena, falling hemoglobin, hypotension, or new neurologic symptoms.
Renal impairment can increase drug exposure.
priorities: Verify dose, indication, weight, renal function, and timing around procedures.
Assess platelet history and bleeding.
Use the prefilled-syringe technique exactly as instructed and avoid unnecessary manipulation of the air bubble unless product instructions specify otherwise.
assessMonitor: Trend CBC/platelets, renal function, bleeding, injection sites, and anti-Xa only when specifically indicated/ordered.
interventions: Rotate abdominal injection sites and avoid rubbing the site after injection.
medicationSafety: Spinal/epidural procedures increase risk of spinal hematoma and require careful timing.
Protamine only partially reverses LMWH anticoagulant effect.
teaching: Demonstrate self-injection technique, report bleeding, and tell clinicians about enoxaparin before procedures.
delegationScope: Subcutaneous medication administration may be within PN scope; renal-dose decisions and neuraxial timing require prescriber/RN/pharmacy coordination.
examTrap: Massaging the injection site after enoxaparin administration.
oneLinePearl: Enoxaparin: abdomen, no rubbing, watch kidneys and bleeding.

title: Clopidogrel: Antiplatelet Bleeding and Procedure Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Clopidogrel inhibits platelet activation and reduces arterial thrombotic events but increases bleeding risk. Adherence is especially critical after coronary stenting; stopping it without cardiology/prescriber direction can precipitate stent thrombosis.
recognize: Bleeding may include easy bruising, epistaxis, hematuria, GI bleeding, or prolonged bleeding after procedures.
Rare thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura can cause thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, neurologic/renal findings, and fever.
priorities: Assess bleeding and confirm peri-procedural instructions.
Escalate new neurologic symptoms, severe bleeding, or suspected TTP.
Reinforce adherence after stent placement.
assessMonitor: Trend CBC, bruising/bleeding, stool/urine, medication interactions, and procedure plans.
interventions: Use bleeding precautions and minimize avoidable trauma.
medicationSafety: Omeprazole and esomeprazole can reduce clopidogrel activation through CYP2C19 inhibition; medication review is important.
Concurrent NSAIDs, anticoagulants, and other antiplatelets increase bleeding risk.
redFlags: Acute chest pain after unplanned discontinuation
teaching: Do not stop clopidogrel on your own, especially after a coronary stent; report abnormal bleeding and tell procedural clinicians before surgery/dental work.
delegationScope: Procedure-hold decisions and suspected TTP require licensed clinician escalation.
examTrap: Stopping clopidogrel for a procedure without confirming the cardiology/prescriber plan after recent stenting.
oneLinePearl: Clopidogrel prevents platelet clots; premature stent-era interruption can be dangerous.

title: Amiodarone: Lungs, Liver, Thyroid, Rhythm
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Amiodarone is a potent antiarrhythmic with potentially serious pulmonary, hepatic, thyroid, cardiac, ocular, and interaction toxicities. New cough/dyspnea, jaundice, marked bradycardia, syncope, visual changes, or thyroid symptoms require prompt evaluation.
recognize: Pulmonary toxicity may present with progressive cough and dyspnea.
Amiodarone can cause either hypo- or hyperthyroidism because of its iodine content and direct thyroid effects.
It can prolong QT and cause bradycardia, although torsades is less common than with some other QT-prolonging drugs.
priorities: Assess rhythm/rate, BP, respiratory symptoms, thyroid/liver history, and interacting medications.
Report new respiratory symptoms or significant bradycardia promptly.
Use specialist-directed monitoring and initiation practices.
assessMonitor: Trend ECG/rhythm, liver tests, thyroid function, pulmonary symptoms/testing, electrolytes, vision symptoms, and interactions.
interventions: Correct potassium/magnesium abnormalities when ordered and reduce avoidable QT-prolonging combinations.
medicationSafety: Amiodarone interacts with warfarin, digoxin, many statins, and other rhythm/QT drugs.
Grapefruit products can alter amiodarone exposure and should be avoided according to product labeling.
teaching: Keep scheduled lung/liver/thyroid/rhythm follow-up and report cough, dyspnea, fainting, vision changes, or jaundice.
delegationScope: IV antiarrhythmic administration and rhythm interpretation vary by competency/scope; toxicity recognition requires licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Treating a new dry cough on amiodarone as trivial without considering pulmonary toxicity.
oneLinePearl: Amiodarone works broadly and can injure broadly—lungs, liver, thyroid, rhythm.

title: Adenosine: Rapid Push for Regular Narrow-Complex SVT
bottomLine: Adenosine transiently blocks AV-node conduction and can terminate selected regular narrow-complex reentrant SVTs. It must be given as a rapid IV bolus with immediate flush under continuous monitoring because its half-life is only seconds.
recognize: Brief flushing, chest pressure, dyspnea, or a transient pause/asystole can occur and may be dramatic but short-lived.
Adenosine is not a treatment for every tachycardia and does not terminate atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter in the usual way.
priorities: Confirm the rhythm and patient stability before administration.
Maintain continuous ECG and resuscitation readiness.
Administer through the closest practical IV access as a rapid push followed immediately by saline flush according to protocol.
assessMonitor: Monitor rhythm conversion, BP, symptoms, bronchospasm, and recurrence.
interventions: Attempt vagal maneuvers first when appropriate for stable regular SVT per protocol.
medicationSafety: Dipyridamole can potentiate adenosine; methylxanthines such as caffeine/theophylline can antagonize it.
Use caution in asthma/reactive-airway disease because bronchospasm can occur.
teaching: Explain beforehand that a brief intense chest sensation or pause can occur because the effect is very short.
delegationScope: IV adenosine administration typically requires advanced rhythm competency and facility-defined scope; the PN role may be recognition, preparation, monitoring, and escalation.
examTrap: Giving adenosine slowly over several minutes instead of as a rapid bolus.
oneLinePearl: Adenosine is fast drug, fast push, fast effect.
sourceBasis: AHA 2025 Adult Advanced Life Support guidance

title: Atropine: Symptomatic Bradycardia Support
bottomLine: Atropine blocks parasympathetic effects and is used for selected symptomatic bradycardia. The clinical target is improved perfusion—not simply a faster heart rate—and pacing or vasoactive support may be needed if atropine fails.
recognize: Symptomatic bradycardia is concerning when associated with hypotension, altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute heart failure.
Anticholinergic effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, and confusion, especially in older adults.
priorities: Assess perfusion and identify reversible causes while preparing emergency treatment.
Administer according to the bradycardia algorithm when ordered/authorized.
Prepare for transcutaneous pacing or infusion therapy if ineffective.
assessMonitor: Continuous rhythm, BP, mental status, chest pain, perfusion, and response.
interventions: Apply pacing pads early when severe bradycardia may require pacing.
medicationSafety: Atropine may be ineffective in some infranodal/high-grade blocks and should not delay pacing when the patient is unstable.
Anticholinergic effects can worsen urinary retention or delirium in susceptible patients.
teaching: In emergency use, explain only what is feasible while prioritizing perfusion and escalation.
delegationScope: Emergency IV medication administration and rhythm interpretation depend on state/facility competency; PN recognition of symptomatic bradycardia requires immediate escalation.
examTrap: Repeating atropine while an unstable high-grade block deteriorates instead of preparing pacing.
oneLinePearl: Atropine is a bridge for symptomatic bradycardia—not a reason to delay pacing.
sourceBasis: AHA 2025 Adult Advanced Life Support guidance

title: Norepinephrine: Vasopressor Perfusion Support
bottomLine: Norepinephrine is a potent vasopressor used to restore perfusion in selected shock states, commonly septic shock after adequate initial fluid resuscitation. Titrate to the ordered hemodynamic target while monitoring perfusion and the IV site because extravasation can cause tissue ischemia.
recognize: Improving blood pressure without improving mentation, urine output, capillary refill, or lactate trend may not represent adequate resuscitation.
Cool pale tissue, pain, swelling, or blanching at a peripheral IV site can signal extravasation.
priorities: Use continuous hemodynamic monitoring and verify infusion concentration/rate.
Assess IV access frequently and use central access when clinically appropriate/available without delaying lifesaving therapy.
Escalate extravasation immediately and follow the reversal protocol.
assessMonitor: Trend MAP/BP, rhythm, extremity perfusion, mentation, urine output, lactate trend when ordered, and infusion site.
interventions: Use a smart pump and dedicated line when possible.
Correct hypovolemia and underlying cause according to the shock plan.
medicationSafety: Excess vasoconstriction can impair peripheral/mesenteric perfusion.
Extravasation management may include local phentolamine per protocol.
teaching: This is an emergency monitored medication; explanations focus on the purpose of supporting blood pressure/perfusion.
delegationScope: Vasopressor titration is generally outside routine LPN/LVN scope and depends on state/facility policy; PN responsibilities may include monitoring, site surveillance, and immediate escalation.
examTrap: Focusing only on the blood-pressure number while ignoring worsening urine output or limb perfusion.
oneLinePearl: Vasopressors raise pressure; the nurse must still prove perfusion.

title: ARBs: Blood Pressure, Potassium, and Kidneys
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Angiotensin-receptor blockers such as losartan lower blood pressure and are used in selected cardiac/renal conditions. Monitor BP, potassium, and renal function, and avoid use during pregnancy because of fetal toxicity.
recognize: Dizziness, hyperkalemia, and renal-function changes are key safety concerns.
ARBs are less likely than ACE inhibitors to cause cough but can rarely cause angioedema.
priorities: Assess BP and ordered potassium/renal monitoring.
Review potassium supplements, salt substitutes, NSAID use, dehydration, and pregnancy status/potential.
Escalate facial/tongue swelling or severe hyperkalemia symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, creatinine/eGFR, potassium, dizziness, edema, and adherence.
interventions: Teach slow position changes and avoidance of unsupervised potassium supplementation.
medicationSafety: Pregnancy exposure can cause fetal harm and requires prompt prescriber contact.
NSAIDs and volume depletion can increase renal risk in susceptible patients.
teaching: Do not use potassium salt substitutes or supplements without approval; report pregnancy promptly.
delegationScope: Interpretation of renal/potassium changes and pregnancy-related medication decisions requires authorized clinician review.
examTrap: Assuming ARBs have no pregnancy risk because they cause less cough than ACE inhibitors.
oneLinePearl: ARB safety mirrors ACE safety on potassium, kidneys, pressure, and pregnancy.
